paper_metadata.title: Provable bounds for noise-free expectation values computed from noisy samples

summary: The paper proves that noisy sampling from quantum circuits can recover noise‑free expectation value bounds using CVaR with sampling overhead √γ rather than γ². Experiments on IBM’s 127‑qubit Sherbrooke device run QAOA up to p=5 (1440 CNOTs) for a 127‑variable higher‑order Ising model and up to p=2 (922 CNOTs) for a 40‑node MAXCUT instance, showing empirical agreement between theoretical CVaR bounds and noisy hardware results.

experiments.description: QAOA for MAXCUT on a random 3-regular graph with 40 nodes, executed on IBM Sherbrooke with depths p=1 and p=2; classical light-cone simulation used to obtain optimal parameters and noise-free reference values.

algorithm.ansatz: standard QAOA ansatz with alternating cost and mixer unitaries
algorithm.optimizer: classical optimization via light-cone simplifications; specific optimizer not reported
algorithm.parameter_initialization: optimal parameters determined classically using light-cone simplifications

problem_formulation.encoding_details: MAXCUT on 3-regular graph encoded as diagonal Ising Hamiltonian / QUBO with one qubit per graph node
problem_formulation.objective_function: maximize cut value (equivalently minimize Ising energy for MAXCUT encoding)
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: MAXCUT Ising Hamiltonian on a 40-node 3-regular graph

problem_instance.description: Random 3-regular graph MAXCUT instance from Ref. [11]
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Circuits run on ibm sherbrooke; p=1 with 10^5 shots and p=2 with 10^7 shots; compare noisy expectation, noise-free expectation from classical simulation, CVaR, and best sampled value

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise; Pauli-Lindblad model used in theory; experiments run without twirling
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: CVaR-based bound; staggered dynamical decoupling; no probabilistic error cancellation in experiments

implementation_details.transpilation_target: IBM Sherbrooke ECR-native hardware; paper reports CNOTs for readability
implementation_details.classical_solver: light-cone optimized classical simulation; CPLEX used only for other experiment
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: classical optimization of QAOA parameters using light-cone simplifications
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: sort samples and compute CVaR; compare to noise-free expectation and global optimum

speedup_claims.factor: sampling overhead reduced from gamma^2 (PEC) to sqrt(gamma) for sampling-based tasks
speedup_claims.conditions: when only sampling bit strings / using CVaR bounds rather than unbiased expectation estimation
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a theoretical overhead comparison, not a runtime speedup; PEC still provides unbiased estimators while CVaR provides bounds.

speedup_claims.factor: provable performance guarantees for QAOA on MAXCUT 3-regular graphs recovered under noisy hardware with sqrt(gamma) sampling overhead
speedup_claims.conditions: for MAXCUT on 3-regular graphs, p=1,2,3 under the paper's noise model and alpha <= 1/sqrt(gamma)
speedup_claims.caveats: Guarantees are bounds on expectation values / approximation ratios, not a demonstrated computational speedup over classical algorithms.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: unknown; paper notes sampling overhead √γ grows exponentially and can exceed brute-force search cost
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Substantially higher layer fidelity; Eq. (D1–D2) show hardware fidelity requirements scaling with QAOA depth to keep √γ below brute-force cost.
limiting_factors: large sampling overhead √γ from hardware noise
exponential growth of sampling cost with circuit depth
classical simulation used to compute parameters and expectation values
problem size (40 nodes) still tractable for classical methods

notes: 40 qubits and ibm_sherbrooke are explicitly reported; p=1 and p=2 are explicitly reported. CNOT counts and shot counts are reported in the text/table.
Authors explicitly state that sampling overhead from noise can exceed brute-force search cost (Appendix D).
No claim of quantum advantage; classical light-cone simulation used for parameter optimization and reference results.

experiments.description: QAOA on a hardware-compatible higher-order Ising spin-glass model with 127 variables, executed on IBM Sherbrooke for depths p=1 to p=5; classical MPS simulation and CPLEX used for reference/parameter transfer.

algorithm.variant: QAOA for higher-order Ising spin-glass models on heavy-hex hardware
algorithm.ansatz: standard QAOA ansatz with cost Hamiltonian including linear, quadratic, and cubic Z terms
algorithm.optimizer: parameter transfer / heuristic classical parameter selection; specific optimizer not reported
algorithm.parameter_initialization: heuristically obtained via parameter transfer from smaller/similar instances; exact initial values not reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Higher‑order (cubic) Ising Hamiltonian on a heavy‑hex graph with coefficients dv, dij, and dl,n1(l),n2(l) ∈ {+1, −1}; cubic terms implemented via parity computation on degree‑2 nodes.
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimize Ising Hamiltonian H = sum_v d_v Z_v + sum_(i,j) d_ij Z_i Z_j + sum_l d_l,n1(l),n2(l) Z_l Z_n1(l) Z_n2(l)
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: higher-order Ising Hamiltonian with linear, quadratic, and cubic Z terms on a heavy-hex graph

problem_instance.description: Random hardware-compatible higher-order Ising spin-glass instance on a 127-qubit heavy-hex graph

dataset_specification.description: coefficients d_v, d_ij, d_l,n1(l),n2(l) chosen from {+1,-1} with equal probability; compatible with ibm_sherbrooke heavy-hex connectivity

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: For each p in 1..5, run 10^5 shots on ibm_sherbrooke; compare noisy expectation values to MPS-simulated noise-free values and global optimum from CPLEX; bootstrap CVaR variance using 10^4 repetitions

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise; Pauli-Lindblad model used in theory; experiments run without twirling
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: CVaR-based bound; staggered dynamic decoupling; bootstrapped CVaR variance analysis

implementation_details.transpilation_target: IBM Sherbrooke heavy-hex native connectivity; paper reports CNOTs for readability
implementation_details.classical_solver: MPS simulation for noise-free reference; CPLEX for global optimum
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: parameter transfer and MPS verification of angles
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: compute CVaR, compare to MPS expectation and optimum, bootstrap variance estimates

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: expectation improves from p=1 to p=4 and worsens at p=5

results.unit: not practically runnable at analytic alpha; implied by alpha values being extremely small

speedup_claims.factor: sampling overhead reduced from gamma^2 (PEC) to sqrt(gamma) for sampling-based tasks
speedup_claims.conditions: when only sampling bit strings / using CVaR bounds rather than unbiased expectation estimation
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a theoretical overhead comparison, not a runtime speedup; PEC still provides unbiased estimators while CVaR provides bounds.
The paper reports agreement with theory and classical references, but does not claim or demonstrate a quantum speedup.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Much higher gate fidelities (current EPLG ≈0.055), drastically reduced γ growth, and far larger shot budgets to satisfy theoretical CVaR bounds.
limiting_factors: very low layer fidelities across the 127‑qubit chip
astronomical theoretical sampling overhead (√γ up to ~10^35 for p=5)
need for classical MPS simulation and CPLEX to verify results
no comparison showing quantum outperforming classical solvers

notes: 127 qubits, p=1..5, and IBM Sherbrooke are explicitly reported. CNOT counts per depth and 10^5 shots are explicitly reported. The circuit depth is inferred from the paper's statement that each QAOA round has CNOT depth 6, so total depth is 6p; this is noted as inferred in the notes.
The paper demonstrates theoretical bounds and noise‑robust CVaR behavior but does not claim quantum advantage.
Classical MPS simulations and CPLEX are used to compute reference expectation values and optimal solutions.
